lead: The best practical tips for making the most of your stay in Valencia sustainably, respecting the environment, supporting the local economy and leaving a positive mark on the city.

Valencia was named European Green Capital 2024, the most important recognition in Europe for urban sustainability. The city has calculated and verified its tourism carbon footprint, and more than 150 businesses have joined the Valencia Tourism Green Pact. Visiting Valencia responsibly is easy: the city is designed for it.
In this guide you will find the most practical tips, organised by category, so that your stay is comfortable, authentic and respectful of the environment and the people who live here.

items.title: Organise your visit by neighbourhoods, not by attractions
items.body: Valencia is a compact and completely flat city: its most interesting neighbourhoods are within walking distance of each other. Structure your itinerary by geographic areas — historic centre, Turia Garden, City of Arts, Ruzafa, Cabanyal — instead of jumping from attraction to attraction all over the city. You will save time and transport money and reduce emissions.
facts: Historic centre: Cathedral, Lonja, Central Market and El Carmen district
Turia Garden and City of Arts and Sciences
Cabanyal, beaches and Ruzafa in the evening
Staying in the historic centre will let you reach most of the attractions on foot, with no need for transport.

items.title: Choose the best time to visit Valencia
items.body: Valencia has a mild Mediterranean climate all year round, but some times of year are better than others depending on what you are looking for. Spring (March–May) and autumn (September–November) are the ideal seasons: pleasant temperatures, fewer tourists and keener prices. Summer is ideal for the beach but can be very hot for walking around. If you come in March, experience Las Fallas, but book months in advance.
facts: Best time: 18–24 °C, Fallas in March, gardens in bloom
Beach weather: 28–34 °C, lively atmosphere, more tourists
Highly recommended: 20–26 °C, peace and quiet and low prices
Fewest tourists: 10–16 °C, Christmas markets and museums without queues
Avoid August if you are sensitive to heat: temperatures can exceed 35 °C and the city is very crowded.

items.title: Download the essential apps before you arrive
items.body: With four apps on your phone you can get around Valencia completely independently, paperless and without printing anything. The EMT Valencia app calculates bus routes in real time. Valenbisi shows bike availability at each station. Metrovalencia gives timetables and lines. And the Visit Valencia app has downloadable guides, maps and an up-to-date cultural calendar.
facts: Bus routes, timetables and stops in real time
Bike availability at all 276 stations in the city
Free, downloadable guides, maps and cultural calendar
If you come by car: pay for parking from your phone
Download the Visit Valencia maps offline before you arrive: you will not need data to find your way around.

items.title: Use the integrated public transport · Móbilis Card
items.body: Valencia’s public transport system integrates EMT bus, Metrovalencia metro, tram and commuter train on a single card: the Móbilis Card. With a 10-trip pass (€8.50) you can combine bus and metro in zone A with unlimited transfers. The Valencia Tourist Card includes unlimited transport from €15.30 and is very good value for stays of 2–3 days.
facts: €8.50 · Bus + Metro in zone A · No expiry
Metro L3 or L5 · 25 min · From €1.50
Forget the car in the city. Parking is scarce and expensive. Public transport reaches every point of interest.

items.title: Get around by bike in the Turia Garden
items.body: Valencia has more than 160 km of cycle lanes and a completely flat city, which makes urban cycling an ideal option for any age and fitness level. The Turia Garden offers 9 km of continuous cycle lane with no cars or traffic lights that connects the Bioparc with the City of Arts. Valenbisi has 276 stations: the first 30 minutes of each journey are free with any pass.
facts: €13.30 · Unlimited for 7 days · 30 min free per journey
From €10/day · No time or station restrictions
9 km continuous with no traffic lights from the Bioparc to the CAC
160 km of network across the whole city and the huerta
If you will be spending several days, the annual Valenbisi pass (€29.21) or the weekly one (€13.30) pays for itself perfectly.

items.title: Stay in the historic centre or in the neighbourhood that interests you
items.body: Your choice of accommodation determines how much transport you will need during your stay. The historic centre (Ciutat Vella and El Carmen district) lets you visit most cultural attractions on foot. Ruzafa is the option for those looking for nightlife and neighbourhood restaurants. El Cabanyal, next to the beaches, is for those who put the sea first. Look for small, local hotels: the economic impact on the city is much greater than with the big chains.
facts: Everything on foot: Cathedral, Lonja, Carmen, Central Market
Liveliest neighbourhood: restaurants, bars and nightlife
For those who put the sea first: beaches and the seafaring district
If you come with children and the plan revolves around the CAC
notes: Check whether the hotel has a sustainability certificate or has joined the Valencia Tourism Green Pact: more than 150 businesses take part.

items.title: Eat seasonal and local · Km 0 produce
items.body: Valencian cuisine has the huerta and the Mediterranean as its direct pantry. Eating seasonal and local is not only more sustainable: it is also tastier and cheaper. The municipal markets are the best place to buy fresh produce. In restaurants, look for those that work with produce from the huerta and, for wines, the DOs Valencia and Utiel-Requena. The Sunday paella in El Palmar, inside the Albufera, is the most authentic experience and as close to kilometre 0 as it gets.
facts: Fresh produce from the huerta straight from the producer
In El Palmar or in restaurants that use DO Valencia rice
DO Valencia and DO Utiel-Requena: great wines at local prices
The most Valencian drink: in a traditional horchata shop in Alboraya
notes: Avoid restaurants with photos on the menu and a menu in several languages next to monuments: they are usually tourist traps serving low-quality food.

items.title: Valencian mealtimes · Learn the local culture
items.body: Mealtimes in Valencia are later than in the rest of Europe. Breakfast is light (café con leche and toast). The main meal is between 14:00 and 16:00: this is when most restaurants have a set menu of the day for €10–15 with starter, main course and dessert. Dinner starts at 21:00 and restaurants do not open before 20:30. Adapting to these times will save you from eating in tourist restaurants.
facts: 08:00–10:00 · Café con leche, toast with olive oil or churros
notes: The menu of the day is the best value in Valencia: starter, main course, dessert, bread and a drink for €10–15. Look for restaurants where the locals eat.

items.title: Respect protected natural areas
items.body: The Albufera Natural Park, the beaches of El Saler and La Devesa, and the inland natural parks have access rules that must be respected. Not entering restricted areas of the Albufera, staying on marked paths, not leaving waste on natural beaches and not disturbing wildlife are the pillars of responsible ecotourism. The Racó de l’Olla has periods of restricted access to protect nesting birds.
facts: Respect the marked limits in the Racó de l’Olla and La Devesa
Do not leave the marked paths in natural parks
Natural beaches have no daily cleaning service
Watch birds from the observatories without noise or getting too close
notes: To get to El Saler or the Albufera, use the public bus or a bike. Cars in summer cause traffic jams and pollute one of Valencia’s most fragile spaces.

items.title: Buy local crafts and authentic souvenirs
items.body: The most sustainable souvenirs, and those with the most history, are those made in Valencia: Manises ceramics, handcrafted fans from Vibenca or Carbonell, silk accessories from Ensedarte, Lladró porcelain or handmade jewellery. Avoid industrially or mass-produced souvenirs made outside Spain. Buying local crafts supports Valencian artisans, keeps traditions alive and leaves a real economic impact on the city.
facts: Manises and Paterna: production centres 10 km from the centre
Vibenca or Carbonell: hand-painted pieces in silk or lace
Ensedarte: hand-painted silk accessories made in Valencia
Founded in Valencia in 1953: the most international Spanish brand
notes: The Central Market, the Plaza Redonda and El Carmen are the best places to find authentic crafts without tourist middlemen.

items.title: Use water and energy responsibly
items.body: Valencia is a Mediterranean city that periodically suffers from water stress. In your accommodation, do not change the towels every day if it is not necessary, avoid long baths and turn off the air conditioning when you leave the room. In natural areas, the water of the Albufera and the province’s rivers is an especially fragile resource that sustains unique ecosystems.
facts: Reuse towels for several days: saves up to 40 litres per wash
Switch off when you leave: summer energy consumption is critical
Valencia’s tap water is drinkable and of good quality
Take your own bag for shopping in markets and shops
Tap water in Valencia is completely drinkable. A reusable bottle eliminates dozens of plastic bottles during your stay.

items.title: Shop in the municipal markets, not in supermarkets
items.body: If you are staying in an apartment or want to pick up something fresh, the municipal markets are infinitely more sustainable than supermarkets: the produce comes direct from the producer or from the Lonja, with no industrial packaging, and the economic impact stays entirely in the local economy. The Central Market, the Ruzafa market and the Cabanyal market are open Monday to Saturday from 7:30 to 14:00.
facts: Bring reusable bags: the markets sell without plastic
Comparable to or better than the supermarket, with higher quality
You can ask the seller the exact origin of the product
notes: Always bring cloth bags to the markets. In Valencia many stalls no longer offer plastic bags, and those that do charge for them.

blocks.title: The responsible traveller’s code in Valencia
items: Get around on foot, by bike or on public transport: the historic centre is entirely pedestrian
Spend in small shops, buy local crafts and eat in neighbourhood restaurants
Use tap water — it is drinkable — and carry a reusable bottle
Do not leave waste in natural areas or on the protected beaches of the Albufera Park
Respect Valencian hours: lunch at 14:00 and dinner at 21:00
Choose local guides for guided visits: the economic impact on the city is direct
